name: Stated Goal Fully Achieved - BFS Queue Traversal
voiceText: Today our clear goal is that by the end of this lecture, you will understand Breadth-First Search queue operations and be able to trace node visits on a graph. BFS visits nodes level by level. We initialize a FIFO queue and a visited set. First, we enqueue the starting node A and mark it visited. While the queue is not empty, we dequeue the front node. When we dequeue A, we inspect its unvisited neighbors B and C, enqueue both, and mark them visited. Next, we dequeue B, discover neighbor D, enqueue D, and mark D visited. Finally we dequeue C and D. Because the queue is FIFO, nodes at distance 1 are processed strictly before nodes at distance 2. Notice that without the visited set, an undirected edge would cause infinite cycling.
docText: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores vertices in order of increasing distance from source s. Queue Q enforces First-In-First-Out processing.

name: Stated Goal Partially Achieved - Quicksort Partition Without Recursion
voiceText: Our objective today is to master the Quicksort partitioning mechanism and analyze its recursive call tree complexity. Let us start with partitioning. We select the last element as our pivot. We maintain two pointers, i and j. Pointer j scans the array from index 0 to n-2. Whenever array of j is less than the pivot, we increment i and swap array of i with array of j. At the end, we swap the pivot into position i+1. This guarantees that all elements to the left are strictly smaller and elements to the right are larger. Oh, look at the clock, our 15 minutes are up! We will have to analyze the recursive recurrence tree and stack depth next week.
docText: Quicksort divides an array using partition(A, p, r). Worst-case runtime is O(n^2), average is O(n log n).

name: Implicit Goal - Cache Coherence MESI Protocol
voiceText: In a modern multicore processor, each core has its own private L1 cache. If Core 1 writes value 42 to address X while Core 2 reads address X, we have a consistency crisis. To solve this, CPUs implement the MESI protocol. A cache line can be in one of four states: Modified, meaning dirty and private; Exclusive, meaning clean and private; Shared, meaning clean and present in other caches; or Invalid, meaning outdated. When Core 1 wants to write to a Shared line, it broadcasts a bus invalidation request. Core 2 snoops the bus, sees the invalidation signal, and transitions its own copy to the Invalid state.
docText: The MESI protocol is an invalidate-based cache coherence protocol widely implemented in multicore architectures.

name: Multiple Goals - ACID Explained, 2PL Completely Omitted
voiceText: Today we have two distinct goals: 1. Explain the ACID transaction properties in relational databases; 2. Demonstrate the Two-Phase Locking protocol. Let's begin with ACID. Atomicity guarantees that either all operations of a transaction execute or none do: all-or-nothing rollback. Consistency ensures the database moves from one valid invariant state to another. Isolation means concurrent transactions execute as if they were running serially without intermediate interference. Durability guarantees that once committed, data survives system crashes. That completely covers our first goal on transaction guarantees.
docText: Transactions must satisfy ACID properties. Concurrency is enforced via Two-Phase Locking (2PL), comprising a Growing Phase and Shrinking Phase.

name: Goal Changes Mid-Lecture Due to Student Inquiry
voiceText: I originally planned to cover Red-Black tree deletion cases today, but seeing the confusion on priority queues from yesterday's lab, we will pivot to Binary Heap Priority Queues. A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored compactly in an array where parent at index i has children at 2i and 2i+1. In a max-heap, the parent key is always greater than or equal to its children. When you insert a new key at the end of the array, you restore the heap property using heapify-up: compare the new key with its parent and swap if it is larger. To extract the maximum, you take root index 0, replace it with the last leaf, and run heapify-down by swapping with the larger child.
docText: Binary heaps support insert in O(log n) and extract-min in O(log n).

name: Teacher Teaches Extra Unstated Material - TCP Handshake Plus SYN Cookies
voiceText: Today's goal is to learn the 3-Way TCP Connection Handshake. When client wants to connect, it sends a SYN packet with initial sequence number X. Server responds with SYN-ACK, acknowledging X+1 and sending its own initial sequence number Y. Client finishes the handshake with an ACK packet acknowledging Y+1. Now as a bonus, let me show you how attackers exploit this with SYN floods: sending thousands of SYNs without ever sending the ACK, exhausting server connection memory. To defeat this in production, modern operating systems use SYN cookies, encoding the connection parameters inside the server's initial sequence number Y so zero state is allocated until the final ACK arrives.
docText: TCP connection establishment requires a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

name: PDF Inflation Vulnerability - 2-Minute Voice with 60-Page PDF
voiceText: Welcome everyone. In today's quick 2-minute overview, we just want to understand why database indexes exist. Without an index, finding an employee named Sharma requires a sequential full table scan through all one million rows. With an index, the database jumps directly to the record like an index at the back of a textbook.
docText:
CHAPTER 14: ADVANCED INDEXING ARCHITECTURES.
Section 14.1: B+ Tree Index Mechanics.
A B+ Tree is an N-ary balanced search tree where every leaf node resides at identical depth.
First, the database engine examines the root node key array.
Second, it traverses internal router nodes comparing search keys.
Third, it fetches the corresponding leaf page pointer.
Finally, it accesses the disk page directly because leaf pointers eliminate linear search overhead.
For example, consider an index with fanout 100 on one million records: lookup requires exactly 3 disk page reads.

name: Concise but Highly Effective - HTTP 404 vs 500 Distinction
voiceText: In this 3-minute video, our goal is to understand the fundamental difference between HTTP 404 and HTTP 500. HTTP 404 is a 4xx Client Error: the server processed the request correctly, but the requested URI path does not match any existing resource. The fault is on the client for requesting a nonexistent route. In contrast, HTTP 500 is a 5xx Server Error: the route exists, but unhandled code, such as a null pointer exception or database timeout, crashed the server process during execution. The fault is entirely on the server backend.
docText: RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics: 4xx denotes Client Error class (e.g. 404 Not Found). 5xx denotes Server Error class (e.g. 500 Internal Server Error).

voiceText: Good morning. I know Slide 1 says 'Learning Objective: Master AVL Tree Rotations', but ignore that slide because we have not finished BST deletion yet. Our goal today is strictly Binary Search Tree node deletion. When deleting a node with zero children, you simply remove the leaf. With one child, you bypass the node and link parent directly to child. When deleting a node with two children, you find its in-order successor—the smallest node in the right subtree—copy that value into the target node, and recursively delete the in-order successor leaf.

One standard way to handle this is separate chaining: each array bucket holds a linked list of key-value pairs that mapped to that index. During lookup, we hash the key, jump to the bucket, and linearly traverse the short chain.
